An octopus is a soft-bodied sea animal with eight arms, found in every [[Ocean|ocean]]. Octopuses are known for their intelligence, their ability to change colour in a fraction of a second, and for squeezing through gaps barely wider than their beak.{1}
An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, and one pumps it around the rest of the body. Its blood is blue because it carries oxygen using copper rather than iron.{2}
Most of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, which can taste and touch at the same time.
Octopuses use tools, open jars and recognise individual people in aquariums. Some species carry coconut shells to use as portable shelters.{3}
They hunt mostly at night, eating crabs, shrimp and small fish.

Octopuses appear in folklore from many coastal cultures, often as giant sea monsters. Modern writers more often celebrate their curiosity. See also [[Lighthouse|lighthouses]], a common setting for sea stories.
Marine Biology Today, “Why octopus blood is blue”, 2023.
Tower that guides ships with light

A lighthouse is a tower with a bright light at the top, built to warn ships of dangerous coasts and guide them into harbour. Each lighthouse flashes in its own pattern so sailors can tell them apart at night.{1}
Early lighthouses burned wood or coal in open fires. Later, oil lamps and huge curved lenses made the light visible from more than 40 kilometres away.{2}
For centuries, lighthouse keepers lived at the tower, keeping the lamp lit and the glass clean. Today almost every lighthouse is automatic.

Sourdough is bread made with a starter — a living mix of flour and water full of wild yeast and friendly bacteria — instead of packaged yeast. The bacteria give it its slightly sour taste and chewy crust.{1}
A starter is fed with fresh flour and water every day. A healthy starter doubles in size a few hours after feeding and smells pleasantly tangy.{2}
The dough rises slowly, often overnight, then bakes in a very hot covered pot so the crust can blister and crackle.
Largest planet in the solar system
Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the solar system — more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. It is a gas giant, made mostly of hydrogen and helium.{1}
The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been raging for at least 350 years. It has been slowly shrinking since the 1800s.{2}
Jupiter has 95 known moons. The four largest can be seen with ordinary binoculars on a clear night.
